scope: This tool estimates your risk of developing type 2 diabetes over the next 10 years. It is a screening aid, not a diagnosis, and does not assess type 1 or gestational diabetes. A blood test interpreted by a clinician is required to diagnose diabetes.
bands.low.label: Low
bands.low.interp: Your estimated 10-year risk of type 2 diabetes is low. That's good news — most of it comes down to habits worth keeping up.
bands.low.nextStep: Re-check every 1–3 years, or sooner if your weight or health changes.
bands.moderate.label: Moderate
bands.moderate.interp: Your estimated risk is moderate. Small, sustained changes now make a real difference at this stage.
bands.moderate.nextStep: Consider a lifestyle review, and ask your doctor about a blood test in the coming months.
bands.high.label: High
bands.high.interp: Your estimated risk is high. This is the level at which health services recommend a check.
bands.high.nextStep: Arrange a blood test (fasting glucose or HbA1c) with your doctor soon.
bands.veryHigh.label: Very high
bands.veryHigh.interp: Your estimated risk is very high. Please don't be alarmed — it means action now is especially worthwhile.
bands.veryHigh.nextStep: See your doctor soon to arrange a blood test and discuss next steps.
emergency.title: These symptoms may need urgent attention
emergency.body: Feeling very unwell with vomiting, drowsiness, fast or deep breathing, or stomach pain can be a sign of a serious problem with blood sugar. Please seek same-day urgent care or go to A&E. We haven't shown a risk estimate because getting checked comes first.
symptomatic.title: Some symptoms are worth checking promptly
symptomatic.body: The symptoms you ticked can be caused by high blood sugar. Whatever your score below, it's worth seeing a doctor soon for a simple blood test. This is not a diagnosis.
reconcile: One of the cross-checks below flags a higher risk than the main estimate. This can happen with weight carried around the middle, and it's worth mentioning at a check-up.
advice.intro: Based on what you entered, these tend to help most:
advice.overweight: Losing even 5–10% of your body weight measurably lowers diabetes risk.
advice.waist: Trimming your waistline matters as much as overall weight — aim to keep your waist under half your height.
advice.smoking: Stopping smoking lowers your risk of diabetes and much else; free support is usually available locally.
advice.inactivity: Building up to regular movement — brisk walking counts — improves how your body handles blood sugar.
advice.family: A family history can't be changed, but it makes the habit changes above especially worthwhile.
advice.hypertension: Keeping blood pressure well controlled protects against the same problems diabetes causes.
advice.general: A pattern of more vegetables, whole grains and unprocessed foods, with fewer sugary drinks, protects against diabetes.
advice.dietSwap: One easy swap: replace refined carbohydrates (white rice, white bread, sugary drinks) with wholegrain or higher-fibre versions.
secondary.heading: Cross-checks
secondary.whtr.healthy: Healthy — waist is under half your height.
secondary.whtr.raised: Raised — worth keeping an eye on.
secondary.whtr.high: High — waist is 60% or more of your height.
secondary.needWaist: Add your waist measurement above to unlock these two cross-checks.
method: ["This tool uses QDiabetes-2018 (Model A), a risk equation developed and validated on 11.5 million people in English general practice. It uses no blood tests. Separate equations are used for men and women, and it carries coefficients calibrated for each ethnicity you can select.","Calibration: because it was built on UK data, the exact percentage is best calibrated for UK residents of any ethnicity. Elsewhere in the world the ranking stays valid (higher inputs mean higher risk), but the precise percentage is less certain — which is why we also show the cross-checks.","Where a value wasn't asked (a UK deprivation score), a neutral average is assumed, so it neither raises nor lowers your estimate.","Symptoms are handled separately and are never mixed into the score. This tool screens for type 2 diabetes only, and is not a diagnosis.","Attribution and licence: QDiabetes-2018 was developed by Julia Hippisley-Cox and Carol Coupland (BMJ 2017;359:j5019). The QDiabetes-2018 algorithm is © ClinRisk Ltd and released under the LGPL-3.0 licence; this page is Lifeline Daily's own implementation of the published equations and is not endorsed by ClinRisk or the NHS. It is screening information, not a diagnosis."]

email.intro: Optional — your result and next steps, sent once to your inbox. We don't store your health details.
email.consent: Email my result to me. I understand this is screening information, not medical advice.
